findings.claim: The budget/indexing check (`if (scanBudget < 0) { ... indexChildrenByKey ... }`) is moved inside the new `else` branch, so it is skipped entirely whenever the first old child matches.
findings.rationale: Previously this ran on every iteration of the `else if` branch. Now a run of head-matches never re-evaluates it. This is probably benign because `scanBudget` can only go negative inside the `else` branch and is reset to `Infinity` in the same block, so it should never be negative on entry to a fast-path iteration. Worth verifying the initialization of `scanBudget` outside this hunk: if it can start at or below 0, the keyed index would never be built and the linear-scan fallback would be used forever. Medium confidence this is harmless.

findings.claim: The child-matching predicate is now duplicated: once inline as `isMatchFirst` and once inside `findIndex`; the two copies must stay semantically identical.
findings.rationale: I compared both forms and they currently agree (NodeString<->NodeString; keyed -> key+tag; unkeyed -> tag only). But this duplication means any future change to the matching rules applied to only one copy will silently produce wrong node reuse, which is hard to debug. Extracting a shared `const matches = (c) => ...` used by both the head test and `findIndex` would remove the risk. High confidence this is a real hazard, though not a bug today.

findings.claim: On a fast-path miss, index 0 is compared twice (once by `isMatchFirst`, then again by `findIndex`, which starts at 0), and the extra comparison is not charged against `scanBudget`.
findings.rationale: Worst case now does N+1 comparisons instead of N, and `scanBudget` is no longer an exact count of comparisons performed, slightly delaying the switch to the keyed index for adversarial reorderings. Low impact; could be avoided by starting the search at index 1 and adjusting the returned index.

findings.claim: `oldVChildren[0]` is read and passed to `isNodeString` without any guard against a hole or `undefined` entry.
findings.rationale: `oldVChildren.length > 0` does not guarantee element 0 is a defined node (sparse array or `undefined` placeholder); `isNodeString` typically dereferences a property and would throw a TypeError. The pre-existing `findIndex` predicate had the same exposure, so this is not a clear regression, but the new code dereferences the head unconditionally for every child. Low confidence this is reachable; flagged only because `first` is used with no null check.
